title: How to Launch a Lending Product: A Step by Step Guide
summary: Launch a lending product by choosing a model, defining the loan, and covering compliance. Then secure capital, set credit policy, and pilot before scaling.
body_markdown:
### What it takes to launch a lending product


To launch a lending product, you choose a lending model, define the loan, and cover compliance and licensing. Next, you secure capital, set credit policy, and build or buy your technology. Finally, you run a small pilot before you scale.


A lending product is any offer that lets customers borrow money, such as a loan or a line of credit. This guide explains how to launch a lending product in seven steps. The same path applies if you are learning how to start a lending business.


In the Fed's 2025 survey, a larger share of applicants sought financing at online fintech lenders. The[Fed small business credit survey](https://www.fedsmallbusiness.org/reports/survey/2026/2026-report-on-employer-firms) shows that share rose "from 17% in the 2020 survey to 29% in the 2025 survey."


That survey drew about 6,500 small employer firms and is a convenience sample. Read it as a directional signal that borrowers are open to new places to get credit.


‍


### Step 1: Choose your lending model


Your lending model decides who funds the loans, who holds the legal risk, and who owns the borrower relationship. Choose it first, because it shapes every step after it.


Most teams start with one of four models. Many grow along the path from[referral to embedded lending](https://www.lendflow.com/post/the-journey-from-referral-to-embedded-lending) , then take on more control over time.


Model How it works Control Economics Compliance burden Capital you need Time to launch


Referral You send customers to a lender's site Low A fee per referral or funded loan Lowest None Fastest


Embedded lending partner A partner's lenders fund loans inside your product Medium Revenue share or fees Shared with the partner None Fast


Bank partnership A bank makes the loans while you run the program High Larger share of loan income High, with bank oversight Some, often to buy loans or cover losses Slower


Own license You lend under your own state licenses Full You keep all interest and fees Highest The most Slowest


Moving lending in house gives you more control and margin. It also adds licensing work, capital needs and headcount.


- **Fit today:** Pick the model your team, budget and risk appetite can support right now.
- **Plan the next move:** Many programs start with a partner and add control once volume proves demand.


#### Embedded lending partner


Embedded lending means offering credit inside your own product, at the moment a customer needs it. With a partner, the partner's lenders review and fund the loans, while the experience looks native to your brand.


This model suits SaaS platforms and marketplaces that want lending revenue without becoming a lender. Many teams use[white label lending platforms](https://www.lendflow.com/post/white-label-lending-platform-guide) , which put your brand on a ready-made borrower flow.


Lendflow's embedded finance customers operate with 80% smaller teams while converting similar funding volumes. Skip long build cycles—Lendflow helps brands launch embedded lending in days with widgets, landing pages and APIs.


#### Bank partnership and own license


In a bank partnership, a bank originates the loans, which means the bank is the lender that makes them. You design the product, find borrowers and often run daily operations.


Bank regulators expect banks to understand and manage the risks of their third-party relationships, including fintech arrangements. The[interagency third-party risk guidance](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/sr2304.htm) notes banks may form relationships with "new or novel structures and features" seen with "some financial technology (fintech) companies."


Regulators issued that guidance in 2023. The[2023 third-party risk guidance](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/sr2304a1.pdf) says a bank's use of third parties "does not diminish its responsibility" to operate safely and follow the law. The guidance itself adds no new requirements for banks.


On Sept 11, 2026, regulators proposed to rescind and replace the 2023 guidance in the[interagency third-party guidance proposal](https://www.federalreserve.gov/apps/proposals/FR-2026-0031-01/details) . Check its current status before you rely on it.


Still, expect a bank partner to review you closely before launch and monitor you after. Common review areas include:


- **Compliance program:** Your policies, staff training, complaint handling and fair lending controls.
- **Financial health:** Your funding, cash runway and ability to cover any losses you agreed to take.
- **Data security:** How you protect borrower data and keep systems running.
- **Oversight:** Who owns risk on your team and how you report to the bank.


With your own license, you are the lender. This path gives you full control, but it takes the most time, money and staff.


### Step 2: Define the product


Defining the product means deciding who borrows, what they get, and what it costs. Write these choices down early, because every partner and vendor will ask for them.


Start with the borrower segment. Consumer lending serves people, while small business (SMB) lending serves companies. SMB credit often fits SaaS and marketplace platforms, since their users are already businesses.


Next, choose the loan type. Common examples of lending products include the financing types Lendflow supports:


- **Term loans:** A lump sum repaid in fixed payments over a set time.
- **Lines of credit:** A credit limit the borrower draws from and repays as needed.
- **SBA loans:** The[SBA 7(a) loan program](https://www.sba.gov/loans/7a-loans/) gives lenders a loan guarantee, with a $5 million maximum loan. The SBA does not lend directly to borrowers.
- **Equipment financing:** Funding to buy equipment, with the equipment often securing the deal.
- **Invoice factoring:** A business sells unpaid invoices at a discount to get cash now.
- **Merchant cash advances (MCAs):** Upfront cash repaid from a share of the business's future sales.
- **Purchase of receivables:** A funder buys a business's future receivables in exchange for cash today.


Then set the amounts, terms and pricing. The amount is your minimum and maximum offer, the term is how long borrowers have to repay, and pricing is the rate plus fees.


Finally, decide if the loan is secured, meaning backed by collateral, or unsecured, with no collateral. Collateral is property the lender can take if the loan is not repaid. A CFPB guide on[secured versus unsecured loans](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_building_block_activities_differentiating-secured-unsecured-loans_guide.pdf) says lenders see unsecured loans as riskier and "may charge a higher rate of interest."


### Step 3: Cover compliance and licensing


Compliance means following the laws that govern how you lend, market and treat borrowers. The model you chose in Step 1 decides how much of this work sits with you.


This section is general information, not legal advice. Work with a qualified lending attorney before you launch.


**State licensing.** According to CSBS, state regulators are the licensing authority for consumer-facing nonbank financial companies, including consumer finance lenders. State and territorial regulators manage these licenses through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System (NMLS).


The[CSBS NMLS annual report](https://www.csbs.org/sites/default/files/reports/CSBS_AnnualReport%202025%20Web%20version_080526_vfinal.pdf) says that in 2025, "more than 34,700 companies held a state license." The same report says those licenses span activities such as mortgage, consumer finance and money services. CSBS also notes that "NMLS itself does not grant or deny licenses."


**Fair lending and adverse action.** Regulation B is the CFPB rule that implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA), a federal fair lending law. The[Regulation B purpose and scope](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/1/) section promotes credit access "without regard to race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, or age."


Under Regulation B, these rules apply to all credit, "commercial as well as personal." A decline is a common example of adverse action. Under the[Regulation B adverse action rules](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/9/) , a creditor must notify an applicant within "30 days after receiving a completed application."


Under Regulation B, the notice must give specific reasons. Saying the applicant missed your internal standards or a qualifying score is "insufficient."


Regulation B also sets business credit notice rules based on the applicant's gross revenues in its preceding fiscal year. For businesses at $1 million or less, Regulation B lets the statement of action be oral or written.


For businesses above $1 million, Regulation B requires notice "within a reasonable time." Written reasons follow if the applicant requests them in writing within 60 days.


Some programs send one application to several creditors. Under Regulation B, a third party may send the notice, but it "shall disclose the identity of each creditor." Our guide to[adverse action notice requirements](https://www.lendflow.com/post/adverse-action-notices) covers these duties in more detail.


**Small business data reporting.** Per the[CFPB section 1071 overview](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/1071-rule/) , Section 1071 requires financial institutions to "compile, maintain, and submit" data on credit applications. That data covers women-owned, minority-owned and small businesses.


Per the CFPB, a May 1, 2026 final rule revised the[CFPB small business lending rule](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/compliance-resources/small-business-lending-resources/small-business-lending-collection-and-reporting-requirements/) to "extend its compliance date to January 1, 2028." Check the final rule text to see if your program is covered.


### Step 4: Secure capital and funding


Capital is the money you lend to borrowers. Your lending model decides whether you need to raise it at all.


$1.5B+ in offers were made on Lendflow in the 12 months ending March 2025. Skip raising a lending fund—connect your borrowers to lenders who are ready to fund.


There are four main ways to fund loans:


- **Partner balance sheet:** A partner's lenders fund every loan, so you need no lending capital.
- **Own balance sheet:** You lend your own cash or equity, which is simple but limits growth.
- **Warehouse line:** A credit line from a bank or fund that you draw on to make loans.
- **Forward flow agreement:** An investor agrees to buy the loans you make, on set terms, over time.


Tie this choice back to your model. Referral and embedded programs usually rely on partner capital, so you can launch without a lending fund.


Bank partnerships may need capital to buy loans from the bank or cover agreed losses. Own-license lenders often start with equity, then add warehouse lines and forward flow as volume grows.


A multi-lender setup, where several lenders review each application, removes most of the capital burden. It also gives borrowers more chances to find an offer.


### Step 5: Set credit policy and decisioning


Credit policy is your written set of rules for who gets approved, for how much, and at what price. Decisioning is the process, often automated, that applies those rules to each application.


The Alabama Cooperative Extension System lists the[five Cs of credit](https://www.aces.edu/blog/topics/finance-career-urban/the-five-cs-of-credit/) as character, capital, collateral, conditions and capacity. It calls them factors used to assess the likelihood of repaying a loan, or creditworthiness. Many lenders build credit policy around this educational framework:


- **Character:** The borrower's track record of paying debts on time.
- **Capacity:** The borrower's ability to repay from income or cash flow.
- **Capital:** Savings or money the owner has put into the business.
- **Collateral:** Assets that can secure the loan.
- **Conditions:** The loan's purpose, amount and terms.


These descriptions are our plain-language summaries, not the source's wording.


Knockout rules come first. These are hard limits that decline an application right away, such as a minimum time in business. Running them early saves time and data costs.


Next, choose your data sources. Most lenders combine three types:


- **Credit bureau data:** Credit reports and scores that show how a borrower has handled debt.
- **Bank data:** Account transactions, shared with the borrower's permission, that show real cash flow.
- **Alternative data:** Other signals, such as accounting, payroll or sales platform data.


Then decide how your engine scores applicants. Our guide to[rules-based vs. machine learning models](https://www.lendflow.com/post/rules-based-vs-machine-learning-credit-models-a-lenders-guide) explains the tradeoffs.


Set a clear approval workflow with three paths: auto-approve, auto-decline and manual review. Every application should land in one path, with a named owner for the review queue.


A decline waterfall sends a declined application to the next lender that might approve it. Lendflow lets lenders build decline waterfalls so no deal leaves money on the table. Its live credit signals, intelligent workflows and AI agents adapt as data flows in.


### Step 6: Build or buy your technology stack


Your technology stack is the set of systems that move an application from start to funded loan, and beyond. You can build each piece, buy it from a vendor, or mix both.


Lendflow's pre-qualified offers drive an average of 42% faster speed to funding. Plan your stack as one connected flow from application to funding.


System What it does Build when Buy when


Loan origination system (LOS) Manages applications from intake to closing Lending is your core product and needs a unique flow You want to launch fast with proven workflows


Decision engine Applies your credit policy and returns a decision You have data scientists and your own models You need rules your team can change without code


Data connections Pull bureau, bank and business data into one place You use only one or two sources You need many sources live quickly


KYC/KYB Verifies people (know your customer) and businesses (know your business) Rarely, since fraud tactics change fast In most cases, from a specialist vendor


Servicing Handles payments, statements and collections after funding Your repayment model is unusual Your product uses standard payment schedules


Software fees are only part of the cost. Our breakdown of the[true cost of a lending program](https://www.lendflow.com/post/build-buy-or-partner-the-true-cost-of-standing-up-a-lending-program) compares building, buying and partnering.

Lendflow automates document handling, communication and decision support, so teams stay lean as volume grows. See how[credit underwriting and decisioning](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/credit-underwriting-and-decisioning) fits into that stack.


### Step 7: Pilot, launch and scale


A pilot is a small, limited launch with a few real borrowers. It is the last step in how to launch a lending product. A pilot lets you test the product and fix problems before you spend on growth.


Run the launch in three phases. Use this checklist to track each one:


Phase Checklist item


Pre-launch Sign partner, bank or vendor contracts


Pre-launch Finalize product terms, pricing and borrower segment


Pre-launch Confirm licenses or bank partner approval


Pre-launch Approve credit policy and have counsel review notices and disclosures


Pre-launch Test every system from application to funding


Pilot Launch to one small segment with a volume cap


Pilot Manually review a sample of automated decisions


Pilot Track core metrics weekly and collect borrower feedback


Scale Open to more segments and raise volume caps


Scale Add lenders, products or channels


Scale Automate the manual reviews that proved reliable


Track four metrics from day one:


- **Approval rate:** The share of completed applications you approve.
- **Conversion rate:** The share of approved borrowers who accept an offer and get funded.
- **Time to funding:** The time from application to money in the borrower's account.
- **Default rate:** The share of loans that stop being repaid as agreed.


To attract borrowers, offer credit where customers already work, such as in your app, at checkout or on invoices. Pre-qualified offers show likely terms before a full application, which makes it easier to say yes.


Use your own channels first, like in-product prompts and email to current customers. Our guide on how to[launch credit products faster](https://www.lendflow.com/post/how-to-launch-credit-products-faster) covers ways to shorten this phase.


### FAQs about how to launch a lending product


### How do you launch a lending product?


You choose a lending model, define the product, cover compliance and licensing, and secure capital. Then you set credit policy, build or buy your tech stack, and pilot before you scale.


### Can I start my own lending company?


Yes, but lending under your own license takes state licensing, capital and a full compliance program. Many founders start with a referral or embedded partner model and add control later.


### What licenses do I need to start lending?


It depends on your product, your borrowers and the states where they live, since state regulators license consumer-facing nonbank lenders. A lending attorney can map the licenses your program needs.


### What are the 5 C's of lending?


The 5 C's are character, capital, collateral, conditions and capacity. This educational framework names the factors used to assess a borrower's likelihood of repaying, also called creditworthiness.


### What are examples of lending products?


Common examples include term loans, lines of credit, SBA loans, equipment financing, invoice factoring, merchant cash advances and purchase of receivables.


### How do I attract loan customers?


Offer credit inside the tools your customers already use, at the moment they need funds. Pre-qualified offers and in-product prompts help turn interest into applications.


### Does a fintech partner reduce a bank's compliance responsibility?


No, under the 2023 interagency guidance, a bank's use of third parties does not diminish its responsibility to operate safely and follow the law. Regulators proposed replacing that guidance on Sept 11, 2026, so check its current status.
